newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-SURPRISED SKAARDAL GETS THE GOLD AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-SURPRISED SKAARDAL GETS THE GOLD AGAIN.

text.p: Atle Skaardal took super-giant slalom gold on Monday to become the first Norwegian to win successive Alpine skiing world titles.

The 30-year-old Skaardal who made his world championship debut in the Italian resort of Bormio in 1985, lived up to his team's nickname of the "Attacking Vikings" and cast aside caution to clock one minute 29.68 seconds.
Compatriot Lasse Kjus, the overall World Cup winner last season but sidelined for much of this one by a long bout of influenza, took the silver medal in 1:29.89.

Wily Austrian Guenther Mader, two years older than Skaardal but competing in his sixth championships compared to the Norwegian's seventh, sneaked in for bronze in 1:30.01 to complete a memorable day for the older generation.
Hans Knauss, Austria's big young hope after winning a super-G in Val d'Isere in December ahead of Mader, was fourth just 0.06 of a second away from the podium.
The top three were all medallists at the last world championships in Sierra Nevada, Spain, last year with Kjus and Mader second and third in the combined there.

"If this is true, if its not a dream I don't think I'll survive today. It's crazy," said a stunned Skaardal, who has not won a World Cup race all season although he finished second in downhills in Chamonix and Val Gardena.

Starting fifth in bright sunshine on a course that last hosted a major race in 1989 when Luxembourg's Marc Girardelli suffered a near-fatal crash, the tall Norwegian carved a fearless line down the Kandahar-Banchetta piste.
And he almost paid for his aggression, teetering alarmingly on his skis on the upper part of the slope.
"Maybe because I was more relaxed I could be more aggressive," the Norwegian said.
His coach Jan Ove Nystuen agreed.
"That's a great day," he said at the finish. "Both (Norwegians) were more relaxed than the others. Atle had already won a title while Lasse had nothing to lose.
"We trained really hard over the summer and the double victory pays us back for all the efforts. This is especially a great day for Lasse after his comeback."
Skaardal was not the fastest man on the piste, that achievement belonged to Norwegian Audun Groenvold who clocked 116.96 kph, but he was the most direct.
Skaardal's victory at Sierra Nevada had been something of a surprise in a career previously short of medals.
He had been a downhill silver medallist in the 1993 championships in Morioka, where the men's super-G could not be run because of bad weather in the Japanese resort.
Kjus, the seventh starter, was the fastest through the initial two intermediates before slowing slightly.
He was almost as stunned as Skaardal to be on the podium but said his form and his confidence had been improving steadily since he returned to the circuit on January 14.

Mader, who had placed second in one of only two super-Gs raced this season and was also runner-up to Kjus in the overall World Cup last year, completed a trio of surprised medallists with his first super-G medal.
The bronze joined five others and one silver accumulated during his world and Olympic career.
"It was a nice super-G, very demanding," the father of two said. "I made a few small mistakes."
There was disappointment for the French, Italians and Swiss who all had high hopes of a medal in the race.
France's Luc Alphand, the downhill World Cup champion and winner of the last super-G in Laax last week, was left out of the top 10 and said he was weak and fighting a cold.
Switzerland's Steve Locher, the first to race, made a blistering start but then blew any chance of a medal with a big mistake on the upper part of the hill.
